chunks: "Whenever the source can be lower than the voltage the load needs. The most common case is a single lithium cell, 3 to 4.
2 volts, powering something at 5 volts, like a USB power bank, a Bluetooth speaker or a handheld device.
Another is two AA or AAA cells, which sit around 2 to 3 volts, feeding a 3. 3 volts microcontroller.
LED drivers are another big one: a string of white LEDs needs 10 to 20 volts or more, but the supply is one battery cell.

Higher up in power, a boost is the standard front end for power factor correction: it takes the rectified mains, which peaks at about 325 volts for 230 volts rms, and holds a bus at roughly 400 volts while shaping the input current into a sine wave.
Solar systems use boost stages to lift a low panel voltage and track its maximum power point, and cars use them to keep rails alive when the battery sags during cranking.
Then there are small high-voltage bias supplies: OLED displays, e-paper, flash units, sensor bias.

The thing I always add is the cost: the battery supplies a bigger current than the load, I out over (1-D) , and that gets worst at the end of discharge, so the design has to be checked at minimum input voltage."
